title: Caer Myrddin to the Esplumoir: the Two Merlins Welded
years: c. 450-c. 577 (traditional; Geoffrey of Monmouth's own conflation of the two Merlins)
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Carmarthen, the church of St Peter: the spirit in the night
stops.campa: In the city of Caer Myrddin, in the church of St Peter, the daughter of the king of Demetia keeps her vows as a veiled nun. She tells her confessors, and will tell Vortigern himself, that a form comes to her by night: a young man of great beauty who embraces her, kisses her, and melts from sight when she signs the cross. He returns again and again, and by him, though she has known no mortal husband, she conceives a child. The wise Maugantius will name such a visitor an incubus, born between the moon and the earth.
stops.quote: There appeared to me a person in the shape of a most beautiful young man, who often embraced me eagerly in his arms, and kissed me; and when he had stayed a little time, he suddenly vanished out of my sight.
stops.quote_source: Historia Regum Britanniae, Book VI (trans. Thompson/Giles, 1848)
suggested_refs: The church of St Peter at Carmarthen, where the king's daughter kept her vows
sources: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae, Book VI
Gerald of Wales, Itinerarium Cambriae (1188), on Merlin's Carmarthen birth

stops.name: Carmarthen, birth and the name given
stops.campa: The child is born within the year, in the town that will one day be called Caer Myrddin for his sake, though later chroniclers will say the town gave the boy his name and not the boy the town. The nuns and the household of the king of Demetia raise him in secret, a fatherless boy in an age that reads fatherlessness as either curse or omen. He grows quick-tongued and strange-eyed, marked from infancy as other than his playmates, though no one yet calls him prophet. The Welsh will remember him as Myrddin; the Latin chroniclers will make him Merlinus.
suggested_refs: Carmarthen (Caerfyrddin), 'Merlin's Fort', the town that bears his name
sources: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae, Book VI
Gerald of Wales, Itinerarium Cambriae, I.5

stops.name: Carmarthen, the quarrel and the search
stops.campa: Vortigern's magicians have told him his falling tower will stand only on ground wet with the blood of a boy who has no father, and the king's messengers ride the length of Britain seeking one. In the streets of Kaermerdin they find two youths quarrelling over a game of ball. One, Dabutius, of proud blood on both sides, taunts the other for having none at all. The messengers seize on the insult, question the bystanders, and learn the fatherless boy's name: Merlin. He and his mother are taken up and carried, under guard, into Wales to stand before the king.
stops.quote: You fool, do you presume to quarrel with me? Is there any equality in our birth? I am descended of royal race, both by my father and mother's side.
stops.quote_source: Historia Regum Britanniae, Book VI (Dabutius to Merlin, trans. Thompson/Giles)
suggested_refs: Merlin's Oak (Priory Street, Carmarthen), the tree by which the town's fortune was bound to his name
sources: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae, Book VI

segments.name: Dinas Emrys: the Dragons under the Hill

stops.name: Dinas Emrys, brought before Vortigern
stops.campa: Vortigern has fled to the mountains of Snowdon, driven from his throne by the Saxons he himself invited in, and labors to raise a last tower on the crag called Dinas Emrys; each night the walls it built by day sink into the ground. The boy Merlin is led up before him with his mother, and hears the magicians' sentence: that the mortar wants a fatherless child's blood. He does not flinch. He asks the wise men, mockingly, whether they know what truly lies beneath the hill, and when they cannot answer, he tells the king to have the ground dug.
stops.quote: Because you are ignorant what it is that hinders the foundation of the tower, you have recommended the shedding of my blood for cement to it, as if that would presently make it stand.
stops.quote_source: Historia Regum Britanniae, Book VI (trans. Thompson/Giles)
suggested_refs: Dinas Emrys hillfort above Llyn Dinas, Snowdonia, where the ruined medieval tower still stands on the summit
sources: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae, Book VI
Nennius, Historia Brittonum, ch. 40-42 (the earliest telling)

stops.name: Dinas Emrys, the pool and the dragons
stops.campa: At Merlin's word the diggers break the hilltop and find, exactly as he said, a hidden pool. Drained, it bares two hollow stones, and within them two dragons asleep, one white, one red. Roused, they rise and grapple in the open air before the king and his court, flame and claw, driving each other back and forth across the drained water. The white gains ground first and the red is pressed to the pool's edge, and the watching Britons groan, for the meaning of a beast the color of their own banner losing ground is not lost on anyone present.
stops.quote: Command the pond to be drained, and at the bottom you will see two hollow stones, and in them two dragons asleep.
stops.quote_source: Historia Regum Britanniae, Book VI (trans. Thompson/Giles)
suggested_refs: The drained pool on the summit of Dinas Emrys, excavated in 1945 and found to hold genuine traces of a filled pool
sources: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae, Book VI

stops.name: Dinas Emrys, the prophecy of the dragons
stops.campa: Weeping, Merlin falls into the prophetic spirit and speaks over the fighting dragons the first of the sayings that will be gathered as the Prophecies of Merlin and pored over for four hundred years. The white dragon, he says, is the Saxon nation Vortigern has planted in Britain; the red is the Briton people, oppressed but not ended. A boar of Cornwall will come to trample the invaders' necks. He turns from the dragons to Vortigern himself: the king's own house will burn around him, lit by the sons of the man he wronged, Constantine, returning at last from Brittany.
stops.quote: Woe to the red dragon, for his banishment hasteneth on. His lurking holes shall be seized by the white dragon, which signifies the Saxons whom you invited over; but the red denotes the British nation, which shall be oppressed by the white.
stops.quote_source: Historia Regum Britanniae, Book VII, the Prophetiae Merlini (trans. Thompson/Giles)
suggested_refs: The Red Dragon (Y Ddraig Goch) of Wales, descended directly from this telling
sources: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae, Books VI-VII
joan_of_arc.journey.json (the Bois Chenu prophecy 'laid to Merlin' draws its authority from this fame)

stops.name: Genoreu (Little Doward), the fire that answers the prophecy
stops.campa: The prophecy keeps its word within two years. Ambrosius Aurelianus and his brother Uther, sons of the king Vortigern once betrayed, land from their Breton exile with an army of the dispossessed. Vortigern flees west again, this time to the fortress of Genoreu on the Wye, in the country of the Ergyng. Aurelius besieges it, fires it, and burns the tyrant inside his own last tower, exactly as the boy foretold at Dinas Emrys. Merlin does not fight in this war; his part was spoken already, in a prophecy now paid in full ash and flame.
suggested_refs: The hillfort of Little Doward above the Wye, identified with Geoffrey's Genoreu
sources: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae, Book VIII
Vortigern Studies, 'Caer Guorthegirn, Little Doward'

segments.name: The Giants' Dance: from Killaraus to Salisbury Plain

stops.name: Amesbury, the vow of Aurelius
stops.campa: King Aurelius Ambrosius, settled on the throne his brother's war has won him, rides to the monastery of Ambrius near the plain of Salisbury, where three hundred British lords lie in a common grave, cut down years before at a false peace-parley by Hengist's men with knives hidden in their boots. Aurelius weeps over the mounded dead and asks his council how best to mark the spot forever. None of the ordinary arts of masons satisfies him. At last he sends for Merlin, the prophet whose fame has followed the fall of Vortigern, and asks him to devise a monument no time can undo.
suggested_refs: Amesbury Abbey, traditionally the 'Cloister of Ambrius' of the Night of the Long Knives
sources: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae, Book VIII

stops.name: Mount Killaraus, the Preseli Hills: the Giants' Dance overcome
stops.campa: Merlin tells the astonished court of a ring of colossal stones on a mountain called Killaraus, carried by giants out of Africa for their healing virtue, each one washed to make a bath that cures any sickness. Aurelius laughs that Britain has stone enough of its own, but sends Uther and fifteen thousand men across the sea under Merlin's direction all the same. They rout the Irish king Gillomanius, who tries to bar the mountain, and Merlin's engines succeed where the soldiers' ropes and levers fail outright: he takes the stones down by an art none of the men can follow, and ships them home.
stops.quote: If you are desirous to honour the burying-place of these men with an everlasting monument, send for the Giant's Dance, which is in Killaraus, a mountain in Ireland. For there is a structure of stones there, which none of this age could raise, without a profound knowledge of the mechanical arts.
stops.quote_source: Historia Regum Britanniae, Book VIII (trans. Thompson/Giles)
suggested_refs: Carn Menyn in the Preseli Hills, source of Stonehenge's actual bluestones, folded by tradition into Killaraus
sources: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae, Book VIII
Bevins et al., geological tracing of the Preseli bluestone source of Stonehenge

stops.name: Salisbury Plain, the Giants' Dance raised
stops.campa: On the plain by the burial ground of Ambrius, Merlin sets the stones up in the very order they stood on Killaraus, laughing, the chronicle says, at the men who had failed to move them by main force: skill succeeds where strength alone despairs. Aurelius, who had mocked the whole scheme when it was first proposed, holds a great feast of Pentecost at the new-crowned ring, gathering the clergy and nobles of the realm to see it. The Britons name it the Giants' Dance, or in later ages Stonehenge, and it stands, as Merlin promised, for as long as the world has yet run.
stops.quote: How is it possible to remove such vast stones from so distant a country, as if Britain was not furnished with stones fit for the work?
stops.quote_source: Historia Regum Britanniae, Book VIII (Aurelius's first objection, trans. Thompson/Giles)
suggested_refs: Stonehenge itself, on Salisbury Plain, still standing where Geoffrey says Merlin set it
sources: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae, Book VIII

stops.name: Winchester, the poisoning of Aurelius
stops.campa: Years into a just reign, while the sons of Vortigern's allies still plot from Germany and Ireland, a Saxon agent named Eopa disguises himself as a physician and comes to the sick king's bed at Winchester with a cup of poison. Aurelius Ambrosius dies as the counterfeit doctor intended, and is carried to the plain he consecrated, to lie inside the ring of stones he raised for other men's dead. The kingdom he leaves is briefly headless. Merlin, who read the dragons truly once, is not present at this deathbed; his part in this generation's grief is still to come, from the sky itself.
suggested_refs: Winchester, traditional site of Aurelius Ambrosius's death by poison
sources: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae, Book VIII

stops.name: Stonehenge, the dragon star and Uther Pendragon
stops.campa: A star appears over Britain trailing one great beam, and at the beam's foot a fiery shape like a dragon, from whose mouth two lesser rays reach out, one toward Ireland, one toward Gaul. Uther, campaigning in Wales, sends for Merlin, who weeps to see it and then explains: the star mourns his dead brother Aurelius; the dragon signifies Uther himself, soon to be king; the ray toward Gaul foretells a son whose power will reach that far. Uther has two golden dragons made for his standards and is crowned Uther Pendragon, dragon's-head, and buries his brother within the stones at Salisbury.
stops.quote: For the star, and the fiery dragon under it, signifies yourself, and the ray extending towards the Gallic coast, portends that you shall have a most potent son, to whose power all those kingdoms shall be subject over which the ray reaches.
stops.quote_source: Historia Regum Britanniae, Book VIII (trans. Thompson/Giles)
suggested_refs: The two golden dragons of Uther's standard, and the name Pendragon it gives his line
sources: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae, Book VIII

stops.name: London, the feast where the passion is kindled
stops.campa: At the Easter crown-wearing in London, Uther Pendragon calls every duke and earl and their wives to his high feast in celebration of a hard-won peace, among them Gorlois, Duke of Cornwall, and his wife Ygerne, said to be the most beautiful woman in the island. The king's eye finds her across the hall and does not leave her again all evening: he sends her dish after dish from his own table, laughs at nothing but her, and pays her such open court that the whole hall marks it. Gorlois sees it too, and before the feast is properly over, leaves for Cornwall without asking leave to go.
stops.quote: No sooner had the king cast his eyes upon her among the rest of the ladies, than he fell passionately in love with her, and little regarding the rest, made her the subject of all his thoughts.
stops.quote_source: Historia Regum Britanniae, Book VIII (trans. Thompson/Giles)
suggested_refs: The Easter crown-wearing feast at London, where the king's passion for Ygerne was first seen by the whole court
sources: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae, Book VIII

stops.name: Tregeare Rounds (Damelioc), the siege
stops.campa: Gorlois's flight is itself an act of defiance, and Uther marches into Cornwall to punish it, laying waste the duke's towns and shutting him up in the hill-fort of Damelioc. For his wife's safety Gorlois sends her further off, to the sea-cliff stronghold of Tintagel, judged the one place in his lands no army could take by force; a narrow neck of rock is its only door. The siege of Damelioc drags on a week without result, the king sick with a longing his soldiers cannot cure, until at last, in despair of any ordinary victory, Uther calls for Merlin, who has followed the army.
suggested_refs: Tregeare Rounds, the triple-ramparted hillfort traditionally named for Damelioc
sources: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae, Book VIII

stops.name: Tintagel, the begetting of Arthur
stops.campa: Merlin offers a medicine no siege engine could match: he will give Uther the exact shape and voice of Gorlois, and his companion Ulfin the shape of Gorlois's man Jordan, so the king can walk into Tintagel as its own lord. Uther swears whatever price is asked. Disguised, the three pass the narrow neck unchallenged, and Ygerne receives the false Gorlois into her bed without suspicion of the fraud, believing her true husband come home from the siege. That same night, unknown to her, the real Gorlois sallies from Damelioc and is killed in the field; and that same night she conceives Arthur.
stops.quote: The same night therefore she conceived the most renowned Arthur, whose heroic and wonderful actions have justly rendered his name famous to posterity.
stops.quote_source: Historia Regum Britanniae, Book VIII (trans. Thompson/Giles)
suggested_refs: Tintagel Castle, its headland split by the sea, the traditional site of Arthur's conception
sources: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae, Book VIII

stops.name: Tintagel, marriage, birth, and the child given over
stops.campa: Word of Gorlois's death reaches Tintagel before Uther can slip away, and Ygerne is amazed to find her husband, as she supposes, at her side when he was reported dead in battle at the same hour. Uther, the fraud no longer of any use, comes to her openly, sues for peace with her kinsmen, and marries her; a son and a daughter follow, Arthur and Anne. Some tellings say the price of Merlin's medicine was the boy himself, surrendered at birth into the prophet's keeping to be raised in secrecy, away from a court where an infant king's life would not be safe.
stops.quote: After this they continued to live together with much affection for each other, and had a son and daughter, whose names were Arthur and Anne.
stops.quote_source: Historia Regum Britanniae, Book VIII (trans. Thompson/Giles)
suggested_refs: The later tradition (Robert de Boron, Malory) of Arthur fostered out at Merlin's arrangement
sources: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae, Book VIII
Robert de Boron, Merlin (the fostering-price tradition, later addition)

stops.name: Arfderydd (Arthuret), the battle and the breaking
stops.campa: A hundred years and more have passed since the child was carried out of Tintagel: the tradition folds two Merlins into one and does not apologize for it. Old now, and far to the north, Merlin serves as bard to Gwenddoleu, lord of Arfderydd, when Gwenddoleu's rivals Peredur and Gwrgi, allied with King Rhydderch of Strathclyde, bring him to battle at Arthuret on the Esk. Gwenddoleu falls. Merlin, who has loved him, looks over a field so thick with the slain that grief itself seems to break something loose in his mind, and in that hour the sane counselor of kings ends and the wild man of the woods begins.
suggested_refs: Arthuret House and Arthuret Knowes, near Longtown, Cumbria, the traditional field of Arfderydd
sources: Annales Cambriae, s.a. 573
Geoffrey of Monmouth, Vita Merlini, ll. 55-95
Myrddin Wyllt tradition, Black Book of Carmarthen

stops.name: Coed Celyddon, the flight and the lament
stops.campa: For three days Merlin will not eat, mourning aloud for the dead of Arfderydd by name, until a new fury takes him and he slips away from the camp to hide in the Caledonian Forest, Coed Celyddon, wanting no one to see him. There he lives wild among the beasts, ruling the deer of the wood as their king, forgetting bread, clothing the ache of memory in verse instead: the Apple-Tree poems, sung to a sweet-boughed tree that shelters him from Rhydderch's search parties, mixing grief for the fifty years of madness still ahead with prophecies of the fall of dynasties yet unborn.
stops.quote: Could injurious fate be so harmful as to take from me so many and such great companions, whom recently so many kings and so many remote kingdoms feared?
suggested_refs: Yr Afallennau ('The Apple Trees'), Black Book of Carmarthen, the wild man's own lament
sources: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Vita Merlini
Yr Afallennau, Black Book of Carmarthen

stops.name: The forest's edge, the stag-ride to Guendoloena's wedding
stops.campa: On a frigid clear night, from a mountain top, Merlin reads the courses of the stars and sees what he himself had permitted: Guendoloena, the wife of his sane years, marries again in the morning. He gathers stags and deer and she-goats into a single line, mounts a stag himself, and at dawn drives the herd before him to the wedding, crying that her presents are looking for her. The bridegroom, watching from a high window, laughs. Merlin wrenches the antlers from his stag, hurls them, and smashes the man's head to pieces; fleeing, he slips at a river and is taken, bound, back toward Rhydderch's court.
stops.quote: At once he wrenched the horns from the stag he was riding and shook them and threw them at the man and completely smashed his head in, and killed him and drove out his life into the air.
suggested_refs: The stag-rider of the Vita Merlini, the image behind every antlered Merlin, lord of the beasts of Coed Celyddon
sources: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Vita Merlini (the stag-ride and the killing of the bridegroom, l. 451 ff.)

stops.name: Alt Clut (Dumbarton Rock), the threefold laugh
stops.campa: Gwenddydd, Merlin's twin sister and Rhydderch's queen, sends a messenger who finds her brother by a forest spring and calms him with harp-music long enough to lead him to court at Alt Clut. There, seated among the nobles, he laughs without explaining why, and Rhydderch, intrigued past patience, offers him his freedom for the reasons. Merlin obliges: a beggar asking alms is secretly sitting on buried gold he does not know he owns; a young man buying leather to patch his shoes will drown before nightfall and never wear them. Both prophecies prove true within the day, and the court is left uneasy at what it has invited home.
stops.quote: He was secretly a rich man and had under him hidden piles of coins.
stops.quote_source: Vita Merlini (trans. J.J. Parry, 1925; Merlin's explanation of the first laugh)
suggested_refs: Dumbarton Rock (Alt Clut), the fortress-capital of King Rhydderch of Strathclyde
sources: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Vita Merlini

stops.name: Hart Fell, the house of seventy doors
stops.campa: Court life chokes him. He refuses Rhydderch's gifts and his queen's company alike and begs leave to go back to his woods, telling the king plainly that the oaks of Calidon please him more than any treasure India produces. Gwenddydd, unable to keep him, has a retreat built for him instead on Hart Fell: a house of seventy doors and seventy windows through which he can watch the stars all night, with scribes set beside him to write down what the turning heavens show. Here he settles for good, half hermit and half observatory, drinking from a spring local memory will call Merlin's Well for a thousand years after.
stops.quote: To these gifts I prefer the groves and broad oaks of Calidon, and the lofty mountains with green pastures at their feet. Those are the things that please me, not these of yours - take these away with you, King Rhydderch.
suggested_refs: Hartfell Spa, the chalybeate spring on Hart Fell still called Merlin's Well
sources: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Vita Merlini
The Merlin Trail, 'Hartfell'

stops.name: Hart Fell, Gwenddydd's colloquy and Taliesin's old grief
stops.campa: Gwenddydd comes to question her brother in his tower of windows, and their exchange is remembered as a poem in its own right: she asks after the fates of kings still to be born, and he answers, calling himself dull of understanding since Arfderydd, uncertain where to turn for delight. Taliesin visits too, and between them they turn over a grief neither has finished mourning: the wounding of Arthur at Camlann, carried by the fairy Morgen to the orchard-island of Avalon to be healed, if healing is possible for a wound so deep. Merlin, who helped beget that king, outlives him by a hundred years and grieves him still.
stops.quote: Since the action at Arderydd and Erydon, Gwendydd, and all that happened to me, dull of understanding I am — where shall I go for delight?
stops.quote_source: Cyfoesi Myrddin a Gwenddydd ei Chwaer (trans. W.F. Skene, The Four Ancient Books of Wales)
suggested_refs: The Isle of Avalon, first named in this form in the Vita Merlini's account of Arthur carried there by Morgen
sources: Cyfoesi Myrddin a Gwenddydd ei Chwaer, Red Book of Hergest
Geoffrey of Monmouth, Vita Merlini, ll. 925-940 (Taliesin's account of Avalon)

stops.name: Hartfell Spa, the new fountain: reason restored
stops.campa: While Merlin and Taliesin sit talking of kings, servants hurry in crying that a new fountain has broken out at the foot of the mountains, pouring pure water through the hollow valley. Merlin sits down on the grass beside it, drinks freely, and bathes his temples in its waves, and at once his reason returns: the long madness leaves him, and he knows himself. He turns his face toward the stars and praises God. When the chieftains come to see the wonder and beg him to take up his sceptre again, he refuses, pleading old age, and stays in the Calidonian forest, serving God in its glades to the end.
stops.quote: At once he regained his reason and knew himself, and all his madness departed and the sense which had long remained torpid in him revived, and he remained what he had once been - sane and intact with his reason restored.
suggested_refs: Hartfell Spa, the chalybeate spring under Hart Fell, the healing fountain of local tradition
sources: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Vita Merlini (the new fountain and the refusal of the sceptre)
The Merlin Trail, 'Hartfell'

stops.name: Stobo, Kentigern's mission
stops.campa: Word of a naked wild man crying prophecies in the woods above Tweeddale reaches Bishop Kentigern, apostle of Strathclyde, who comes in person to Stobo seeking him. Under another name now, Lailoken, the tradition folds him further still, calling him a fool for Christ rather than a fallen bard, though the tale-tellers of later centuries will not trouble to keep him apart from Myrddin. He confesses that he has done penance for a great sin committed in his madness and begs the Sacrament, which Kentigern, moved, administers with his own hand in the little church, though he warns the wild man that death is near.
suggested_refs: Stobo Kirk, in Tweeddale, where local tradition places Merlin's last communion
sources: Jocelyn of Furness, Vita Kentigerni (c. 1180)
Vita Merlini Silvestris (attrib.)
The Merlin Trail, Stobo/Drumelzier itinerary

stops.name: Tinnis Castle (Dun Meldred), the threefold death foretold
stops.campa: Three times, the story runs, the wild man returns to a lord's court begging the same mercy and is driven off with mockery each time; three times he answers that he will die a threefold death before the year turns: crushed under stones and cudgels, pierced through by a sharpened stake, and drowned, and that all three will happen at once. The shepherds of a local king, still smarting from an old grievance, hear him foretelling his own end near the stronghold on the hill above Drumelzier and follow him down toward the river with staves in their hands, meaning to see how true a prophet he really is.
suggested_refs: Tinnis Castle, the hillfort above Drumelzier associated with the local king Meldred
sources: Jocelyn of Furness, Vita Kentigerni
Fordun, Chronica Gentis Scotorum, on the threefold death

stops.name: Drumelzier, the death at the meeting of the waters
stops.campa: At the place where the small burn called Powsail runs into the river Tweed, the shepherds catch him and beat him with stones and staves; falling, he pitches down the bank onto the sharpened stake of a fisherman's trap, is driven through, and drowns face-down in the current before blow or stake alone can finish him. All three deaths he named come true together, exactly as he said. The country people bury him at the confluence itself, and for centuries after point out Merlin's Grave there, repeating the rhyme that ties the meeting of Tweed and Powsail to a union of two crowns still centuries away.
stops.quote: When Tweed and Pausayl meet at Merlin's grave, Scotland and England shall one monarch have.
stops.quote_source: Border folk rhyme, recorded by later antiquarians (Pennant, Chambers) at the traditional grave site
suggested_refs: Merlin's Grave at Drumelzier, on the Tweed at its meeting with the Powsail Burn
sources: Jocelyn of Furness, Vita Kentigerni
Fordun, Chronica Gentis Scotorum
Drumelzier local tradition and the National Record of the Historic Environment entry

segments.name: The Tomb in the Forest: Esplumoir and Glass Isle

stops.name: Fontaine de Barenton, Brocéliande: Viviane
stops.campa: Other tellers will not have him die by a stream in the Border hills at all. In their telling, sworn to just as firmly, Merlin crosses instead into the forest the Bretons call Brocéliande, where a fountain called Barenton boils cold water over a red stone and can call up storms if a knight strikes it with his glove. Here he meets Viviane, a maiden as sharp as she is beautiful, and loves her past all his own wisdom's warnings. Over seasons of walking with her among the oaks he teaches her charm after charm, holding nothing back, until she knows enough magic to keep him.
suggested_refs: The Fontaine de Barenton, in the forest of Paimpont, said to raise storms
sources: Robert de Boron, Merlin (early 13th c.)
Prose Lancelot-Grail Vulgate cycle, the Estoire de Merlin
Destination Brocéliande, site tradition

stops.name: The Tomb of Air, Brocéliande: the enchantment
stops.campa: Under a blossoming hawthorn, deep in the forest, Viviane at last turns the last spell he taught her back upon its teacher, weaving nine circles about him with her scarf as he sleeps, and shuts him inside a tower that has no walls anyone else can see: air itself made solid around him, a cage without bars, invisible and unbreakable. Some call it a tomb; the earlier romance calls it an esplumoir, a mews where a hawk is shut to molt its old feathers and come out new, built by his own hand, into which he withdraws at the last and is not seen among the living again.
suggested_refs: The Tombeau de Merlin, a Neolithic gallery grave at La Marette near the hamlet of Landelles, Paimpont, identified with the site since the 12th century
sources: Prose Merlin / Vulgate cycle, the entombment by Viviane
Didot-Perceval (early 13th c.), the Esplumoir Merlin
Félix Bellamy, La Forêt de Bréchéliant (1896)

stops.name: Bardsey Island, the glass tower
stops.campa: North Wales tells the ending otherwise again, and both tellings are kept: that Merlin took the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain, the ship of Nefyd, the flying woman's mantle, the halter and the hamper and the chessboard among them, and sailed to the holy island of Enlli, the Isle of Twenty Thousand Saints, off the tip of the Llŷn. There he raised a house of glass, Tŷ Gwydr, and shut himself inside with the treasures and, some say, nine attendant bards, to wait rather than to die: sleeping, not buried, keeping the Island's own wonders safe until the day they and their king are needed again.
suggested_refs: Bardsey Island (Ynys Enlli), 'the Isle of Twenty Thousand Saints', off the Llŷn Peninsula
sources: Elis Gruffydd, Chronicle (16th c.), the glass house tradition
Mysterious Britain & Ireland, 'The Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain'

stops.name: Bryn Myrddin, Carmarthen: the circle closes
stops.campa: And Carmarthenshire, closest of all to the beginning, keeps its own ending: that the Lady of the Lake shut him not in Brittany nor on Enlli but in a cave under Bryn Myrddin, the hill two miles up the Tywi valley from the town of his birth, where travelers still say they have heard him groaning under the turf. Whichever telling is believed, or all of them together, the town's old rhyme stands as its own kind of oath: should Merlin's Oak ever fall, Carmarthen is doomed to follow it down. The prophet who began fatherless in this valley is given back to it at the last.
stops.quote: When Merlin's Oak shall tumble down, then shall fall Carmarthen town.
stops.quote_source: Carmarthen local prophecy, attached to Merlin's Oak (Priory Street), recorded by 19th-century antiquarians
suggested_refs: Bryn Myrddin (Merlin's Hill), and the relic of Merlin's Oak preserved in St Peter's Civic Hall, Carmarthen
sources: Mysterious Britain & Ireland, 'Bryn Myrddin'
Wikipedia, 'Merlin's Oak'
Carmarthenshire local tradition
